title: Data and Code for: The Socio-Economic Benefits of Hurricane Forecasting Augmented Observations
abstract: Replication package for the NOAA final report on the socio-economic value of augmented aircraft observations in hurricane forecasting. The package links the data-denial experiments of Ditchek et al. (2023) for eight 2017-2020 continental-US landfalling hurricanes to a county-level structural cost framework spanning 37 hurricanes from 2005-2024. It reconstructs the marginal cost of forecast error, the precision gain from dropsonde assimilation, and the implied retrospective social value of the NOAA reconnaissance fleet. Inputs combine NOAA hurricane forecast and verification data, the Ditchek (2023) HWRF ALL-vs-NO denial archive, FEMA Public Assistance data, BEA county income and GDP data, U.S. Census ACS and TIGER products, SEER tract population data, and SHELDUS hazard-loss data.
purpose: To quantify the social value of in-situ dropsonde reconnaissance data assimilated into hurricane forecast models, and to provide a reproducible benefit-side benchmark for NOAA's aircraft recapitalization decisions.

geographic_coverage_specific: Continental United States counties (3,073 county FIPS) exposed to landfalling hurricanes 2005-2024.
temporal_resolution: Event-based hurricane forecasts and county-hurricane observations; supporting annual demographic and economic inputs.
data_format: RDS, CSV, TEX, PNG; raw inputs in CSV and ZIP archives.
collection_methodology: The replication package is assembled in two parallel pipelines. The VOI pipeline (code/cleaning_voi/) reconstructs the 37-storm county-hurricane panel from public and restricted sources following the conventions of Molina and Rudik (2026). The denial pipeline (code/cleaning_denial/) processes ALL-vs-NO HWRF model outputs from Ditchek et al. (2023) into a county-level forecast-uncertainty panel for the eight landfalling 2017-2020 hurricanes. Both pipelines are orchestrated via a Makefile that produces analysis-ready datasets and all manuscript figures and tables.
uncertainty_quantification: Includes ex-ante forecast standard deviation (wind_fc_sd), squared demeaned forecast error, Conley spatial HAC standard errors (400 km bandwidth) on the primary structural regression, and two-way county and state-by-hurricane cluster-robust standard errors on robustness tables.
data_processing: R scripts clean raw source files, harmonize identifiers, construct forecast exposure variables, merge economic and demographic covariates, and generate the analysis-ready file data/clean/final_dataset.rds and the denial-side data/clean_denial/forecast_denial_data_with_lead_times.csv. NOAA_report.r produces all manuscript tables and figures (Stage 0 data tables plus Stages 1-4 including the cost-benefit benchmark against the 2016 ANSER AoA). appendix.r produces beta and delta robustness tables and per-storm value decomposition.
provenance: Built in 2026 from a canonical reconstruction of the Molina and Rudik (2026) replication package. The 31-storm overlap is byte-identical to the source repository for wind_error, precip_error, and sheldus inputs; FEMA records are a hybrid of the source pull and a March-2026 OpenFEMA refresh covering the six new (2023-2024) storms. Source decisions are documented in the repository README and git history.
integration_with_other_data: County-level forecast, damage, expenditure, demographic, and spatial inputs are linked using FIPS codes, hurricane names, and event dates. The denial panel joins to the VOI panel via hurricane name and county FIPS.
file_size: Approximately 7 GB raw inputs, ~100 MB cleaned outputs.
software_dependencies: R 4.3+ with renv-managed package dependencies (tidyverse, data.table, fixest, conleyreg, modelsummary, kableExtra, sf, here, patchwork, broom). Pipeline reproducible via `make all` from repository root.
access_restrictions: Code is shared via the repository. Most raw inputs are publicly distributed (FEMA, BEA, Census, SEER, NOAA). SHELDUS requires a subscription and is not publicly redistributed. Ditchek (2023) HWRF denial archive is shared by the authors with permission.
retention_policy: Code and metadata are preserved in the public repository. Restricted-access inputs are preserved privately for at least five years after publication; the authors affirm reasonable support for replication and clarification requests.
